transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’ve just gotten a little overextended. I’m an artist, and lately I’ve been saying yes to a lot—more projects, some workshops, fixing up my studio, taking client calls—and at first it felt productive, you know? Like I was finally getting things moving.

But now I’m realizing I may have taken on more than I can realistically manage. The deadlines are piling up, and with the mortgage… it’s starting to feel like it’s closing in a bit. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing you mean, but that’s why I thought I should come in.
During this period, have you been feeling unusually up or energized compared with your normal self?

Yes… I mean, I think so. It didn’t feel like a problem at first—it felt sort of wonderful, honestly. Most days I felt unusually buoyant, like everything was finally coming together in the studio and even out in the garden.

I probably was more “lit up” than usual. But I don’t want to make it sound dramatic. I was just very energized and excited about my plans… though, if someone questioned them or brought up invoices, I could get sharp pretty quickly. I’m not proud of that.
During this energized period, did you need less sleep than usual?

I’m not completely sure. I mean, I was busy and probably staying up later than I should have, but I don’t know if I’d say I needed less sleep, exactly.

I wasn’t really tracking it. I just kept thinking, “I’ll finish this one thing,” and then it would be later than I meant. But I don’t want to overstate it—I’m not sure that counts, does it?
During that energized time, did you feel unusually confident or as if you had special abilities beyond your usual self?

Maybe a little, yes. I don’t want to make it sound grandiose, but… I did have this very strong feeling that my illustration work could be something journals had been missing for years—like a whole visual language for scientific ideas.

And I felt strangely certain that I was the person who could do it. Saying that out loud sounds… a bit much, doesn’t it? But at the time it felt more like clarity than arrogance.
During that energized time, were you talking more than usual?

Yes… probably. I wouldn’t say I was trying to dominate conversations, but in meetings I did notice myself going on and on—faster than usual—about layouts and pigments and symbols and even budgets, all mixed together.

People sometimes had to interrupt me, I think because I wasn’t really leaving them space to answer. That sounds a little embarrassing when I say it, but… yes, I was talking more than usual.
During that energized period, were you more active than usual or taking on more projects than you typically would?

Yes… I think that’s probably fair. I mean, I saw it at the time as being productive, not excessive, but I was taking on a lot more than usual.

I started saying yes to extra illustration projects, planning workshops, trying to reorganize parts of my studio, and scheduling more client calls than I could really keep up with. It all felt manageable when I agreed to it, like I was just finally getting things moving.

But now the deadlines are stacking up, and… honestly, with the mortgage and everything, it’s starting to feel like it’s closing in on me. I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean, but yes, I was definitely more active than I usually am.
During that energized period, did it cause serious problems in your life, like at work, with money, or in your relationships?

I suppose… yes, though I wish I could say it was just “a busy patch.” It has caused some real problems.

A few of my illustration deadlines have slipped, and colleagues have had to check in on me more than once, which is embarrassing because I’m usually very reliable. And… financially, I overcommitted. I spent money I really should have kept aside to keep the studio secure, and now the mortgage feels… at risk.

I don’t like admitting that. I know it sounds irresponsible. But yes, it’s gone beyond just being energetic or ambitious.
How long did that unusually energized, buoyant period last?

It’s been… longer than I’d like to admit, I suppose. Around three months, I think.

It seemed to start after I took on the mortgage for the cottage-studio. At first I told myself it was just excitement and motivation, you know, having a proper space and a reason to push forward. But looking back, that buoyant, driven feeling has been going on since then—so yes, about three months.
During that energized period, were you ever hospitalized because of it?
No, I wasn’t hospitalized for it. It’s been difficult, and I know it probably sounds messy, but it didn’t get to the point where anyone admitted me or anything like that.
During that energized period, did you ever have experiences that others said weren’t real, such as hearing voices or having beliefs that others found clearly unrealistic?

I… not voices, no. But there was something, and I feel a bit foolish saying it.

I became really sure that a couple of clients—and even one editor—were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the system I was working on. They told me they weren’t, and people reassured me, but it didn’t really settle me at the time. It felt very real then, even if now I can hear how extreme it sounds.
Did that belief that clients or the editor were trying to get access to your sketches happen only during the energized period?

Yes… as far as I can tell, it was only during this keyed-up stretch, the whole studio period.

Before that, I mean, I’d worry about contracts or whether someone might use my ideas unfairly, but it was more normal worry, I think. I didn’t feel certain people were plotting or trying to get into my sketches like that.

And I haven’t had voices or visions outside of this, either. Is that the kind of distinction you mean?
